title: The heart among dharma's roots
word: with the Keeper's framing of what
hookLine: Yudhishthira at the yaksha's lake: what is the path? and a law book that names the heart among dharma's roots
carry: the heart is a root of dharma
tomorrow: so is weighing it all just picking and choosing?

lines: THE WAY THE GREAT HAVE WALKED.
cards: Yudhishthira's four brothers lie still beside a lake. Each one drank before answering the voice that guards it. Now the voice, a yaksha, puts its questions to him, and his brothers' lives hang on the answers.
One of them: what is the path? He answers, in paraphrase: reasoning doesn't settle it; the scriptures differ; no single sage's word is final; the truth of dharma is hidden in a cave.
The path is the one the great have walked. The yaksha is pleased, and in the end gives all four brothers back.

teach.b: The Manusmriti says something close, and then goes one step further. Its second chapter opens by calling dharma what good people, free of hatred and grasping, approve in their hearts. Then it names the roots of dharma.

teach.h: FOUR ROOTS: VEDA, SMRITI, THE GOOD, THE HEART.
teach.b: In paraphrase: the Veda, the smriti, the conduct of good people, and what is pleasing to one's own self. Four roots, and the last is the surprise. Commentators call it atmatushti, the self's contentment.
Readers take it in different ways. Some read it narrowly: it counts only where the first three leave a choice open. Others hear in it a place for conscience inside the tradition.
A neighbor tradition says something close.

In his letter to the Romans, Paul writes of people who don't have the law yet do what it asks, and who, in the King James words, "shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness."

teach.h: THE HEART IS A ROOT OF DHARMA.
teach.b: An honest difference: Paul speaks of people outside the law; Manu puts the heart inside a law book, last of four roots. Both leave room for the heart.
So when a rule and your gut pull apart, the Hindu answer isn't 'just follow your gut'. It's the Veda, the remembered books, the way the good have walked, and then a heart shaped by them.

how: Hindu teachers sometimes point to Manu's list of the roots of dharma, the Veda, tradition, good conduct and the self's contentment, when talking about conscience in Hindu ethics; some Christians turn to Romans 2:14–15 when they speak of conscience.

games.q: what does “with the keeper's framing of what” mean?
o: a fast kept to make the heart clean and still
a hymn sung at the opening of a royal court
what a tradition keeps, weighed by the heart too

games.q: roots and hearts — tap the pairs.
p: the path is the one the great have walked
the law written in their hearts

s: a law book like the Manusmriti leaves no room for the heart
it names what is pleasing to one's own self among the roots of dharma.
Paul writes of people without the law who show it written in their hearts
Romans 2:14–15: their conscience also bearing witness.

games.q: nothing in your job's handbook settles a choice, and one option sits badly with you. on the narrow reading of Manu's fourth root, what counts?
o: where the other roots leave a choice, what sits right with you can decide.
your feeling overrules every written rule, always.
feelings never count; only the written rule does.
games.why: on the narrow reading, atmatushti counts where the Veda, smriti and good conduct leave a choice open; other readers hear more room for conscience.

practice: Close your eyes, and bring to mind one choice in front of you right now. Without deciding anything, notice what sits easy in your heart and what doesn't, the way you'd notice warm air and cool.
If you pray, you can hold the choice before God.

wordCard.voice: Kept and rejected, weighed by a root inside the law: atmatushti, the self's contentment, last of Manu's four roots of dharma.

orig.note: Sanskrit atmatushti, the self's contentment: the last root of dharma in Manu's list.

carryVoice: Your line: the heart is a root of dharma, atmatushti, last of four, after the Veda, the remembered books and the way of the good. More tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Aranyaka Parva, the yaksha's questions (Yudhishthira: reasoning is unsteady, the scriptures differ, no single sage is final, the truth of dharma is hidden in a cave; the path is the one the great have walked)
Manusmriti 2.1 (dharma followed by the learned and good, free of hatred and passion, and approved in their hearts)
Manusmriti 2.6 and 2.12 (the roots of dharma: Veda, smriti, the conduct of the good, and what is pleasing to oneself)
